Your video

The example: Blindspot Backgammon

A backgammon coach for your phone. From your own games it names the one costly mistake you keep making, explains it in plain words, and drills your own positions until it disappears.

For: players who see their blunders and still don’t improve.

Free · no account · works offline.

Blindspot Backgammon, PRODUCT.md (Product Purpose, Users). arpadtamasi.github.io/backgammon

Five kinds of video

Kind How it runs
Launch video hook → promise → three features → name and address
Product tour one complete task, through the real screens
Teaser (9:16, 20 s) the problem → two beats → name and address
Explainer a question → the idea, one layer at a time → the sentence to remember
Future pacing imagine → the name → the pain goes → the outcome → the address

The hook speaks the viewer’s language. The promise lands by the second beat. One idea per beat. End on the name and one action.

hyperframes.heygen.com: guides/product-launch-video, guides/faceless-explainer, prompting/examples; the product-launch-video skill, story-design.md.

1 · Launch video: hook, promise, three features

How it runs: hook → promise → three features → name and address.

Why this order: the viewer’s problem first, so they care; the promise second, so they know what it is; then three proofs, each a real screen.

Works for: a program with three things a user gets.

Watch out: each feature is something the viewer gets, not a menu item. Name the kind of program early: here, “a backgammon coach”.

HyperFrames, guides/product-launch-video: “hook stating the problem → 3 feature beats … → end card with logo + CTA”.

1 · Launch video: the video

Music: “Wholesome”, Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0.

2 · Product tour: one task, start to finish

How it runs: one complete task, on the real screens, in order.

Why it works: the viewer sees exactly what using it is like, from the first tap to the result.

Works for: a program with one core task that is quick to show.

Watch out: one task only; a second one makes it a feature list. Use screens from one run, so the board does not change between beats.

HyperFrames, guides/product-launch-video: “Product tour: one complete task through the real screens”.

2 · Product tour: the video

Music: “Wholesome”, Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0.

3 · Teaser, 9:16: the problem, two beats, the name

How it runs: 20 seconds, portrait, for a feed.

Why it works: one problem, two beats, the name. Nothing to read while scrolling.

Works for: a short post where people scroll past.

Watch out: three words per caption. Keep text in the middle of the frame: on TikTok and Reels the app’s buttons cover the bottom.

HyperFrames, prompting/examples: teaser “0–4s problem in one line, big type; 4–16s two feature beats … three-word caption; 16–20s logo + … end card”.

3 · Teaser: the video

Music: “Wholesome”, Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0.

4 · Explainer: one idea, one layer at a time

How it runs: a question → the mechanism, layer by layer → the sentence to remember.

Why it works: if they understand the idea, they want the tool.

Works for: programs whose value is an idea: a method, a measurement, a way of looking.

Watch out: the main idea is clear by the second scene. Keep the opening question short: ours had 13 words for 4 seconds, too many.

HyperFrames, guides/faceless-explainer: “Understand one idea (open with a question, reveal the mechanism one layer at a time)”; “One idea per scene”.

4 · Explainer: the video

Music: “Wholesome”, Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0.

5 · Future pacing: imagine, then the name

How it runs: imagine → the name → the pain goes → the outcome → the address.

Why it works: it shows where the program is going, not only where it is.

Works for: projects with a clear next step; your demo day ends with “what’s next” anyway.

Watch out: start and end on what works today; the vision frame says “Illustration”.

product-launch-video skill, story-design.md: “Future Pacing: imagine → name product → remove pain → mechanism → outcome → CTA”.

5 · Future pacing: the video

HyperFrames: a video is a web page

<div data-composition-id="main" data-width="1080" data-height="1920"
     data-start="0" data-duration="20">
  <div class="clip" data-composition-src="compositions/hook.html"
       data-start="0" data-duration="4"></div>
  <div class="clip" data-composition-src="compositions/named.html"
       data-start="4" data-duration="6"></div>
  …
</div>
  • When: data-start and data-duration on every scene and element.
  • Rendering: headless Chrome steps to each frame and takes a picture; FFmpeg joins them into an MP4. The same input gives the same video.
  • Formats: 16:9 for a page, 1:1 for a feed, 9:16 for Shorts and Reels.

github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes, README: “How It Works”; hyperframes.heygen.com, guides/product-launch-video. The snippet is from our teaser’s index.html, shortened.

What it builds from: skills, blocks, templates

Skills for your agent /hyperframes, /hyperframes-cli, /hyperframes-registry, /media-use …
Blocks, about 450 captions, transitions, kinetic type, charts, maps
Templates play-mode, product-promo, kinetic-type, decision-tree, swiss-grid, warm-grain, nyt-graph, vignelli
frame.md your page’s design system, rewritten for video
Commands init · preview · check · render

It needs Node 22+ and FFmpeg. Your agent runs the commands; you look at the frames.

hyperframes.heygen.com: catalog, examples; github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes, README.
